q: What does compliance mean in business?
r: Following the laws, rules and standards that apply to the business
It reduces legal and financial risk.
w: Choosing the lowest prices to attract more customers each month
Hiring as many employees as the budget will allow
Advertising on as many platforms as possible

q: What is a regulation?
r: A rule made by a government agency that businesses must follow
Agencies write regulations to carry out laws.
w: A suggestion that businesses may ignore if they prefer
A discount offered to businesses that pay taxes early
A contract between two private companies

q: What is the purpose of a compliance officer?
r: To make sure the company follows laws and internal policies
They monitor, train and report on compliance.
w: To set the prices that customers pay for products
To design advertisements for the company's products
To repair equipment used in the company's factory

q: What is a code of conduct?
r: A written set of rules for ethical and professional behavior
Employees may be required to follow it.
w: A secret list of passwords used by managers
A schedule of employee shifts for the month
A list of products offered by the company

q: An employee accepts an expensive gift from a supplier who wants a contract. What compliance issue does this raise?
r: A possible conflict of interest or bribery concern
Gifts can influence decisions improperly.
w: A way to lower company costs

q: What is whistleblowing?
r: Reporting illegal or unethical activity inside an organization
Laws protect many whistleblowers.
w: Spreading false rumors about a coworker
Asking a manager for a raise

q: What is the Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA)?
r: An agency that sets and enforces workplace safety standards
Employers must provide safe workplaces.
w: An agency that collects income taxes from workers
An agency that approves new drugs for sale
An agency that sets interest rates

q: A warehouse worker is injured because required safety guards were removed. Which agency may investigate?
r: OSHA
It enforces workplace safety rules.
w: It does not handle workplace safety.

q: What does the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) enforce?
r: Laws against workplace discrimination
It handles complaints about unfair treatment.
w: Laws that set the minimum prices of goods
Laws that control imports and exports

q: A manager refuses to hire a qualified applicant because of the applicant's religion. What is this?
r: Illegal discrimination
Hiring decisions must not rest on protected traits.
w: It is not related to tax.

q: What is the Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA) mainly about?
r: Minimum wage, overtime and child labor rules
It sets basic pay standards.

q: A non-exempt worker earns $14 an hour and works 44 hours. Overtime is 1.5 times pay after 40 hours. What is total pay?
w: That pays all hours at the normal rate.
That pays all hours at overtime rate.

q: What is the purpose of record keeping for compliance?
r: To prove that the company followed required rules
Records support audits and investigations.
w: To increase the number of forms employees fill out
To raise product prices for customers

q: An audit finds missing safety training records. What is the best response?
r: Complete the training, fix the records and set up a tracking system
It corrects the gap and prevents repeats.
w: Destroy the audit report so no one sees it
Blame the auditor for the finding
Ignore the finding until the next audit

q: What is a license?
r: Official permission to operate a business or practice a profession
Governments issue licenses.
w: A discount for buying in bulk

q: A restaurant opens without a required health permit. What is the likely result?
r: Fines or closure by the authorities
Operating without a permit breaks rules.
w: A reward from the health department

q: What is data privacy compliance?
r: Following laws that protect personal information
Examples include GDPR and CCPA.
w: Sharing customer data with anyone who asks
Selling personal data without telling customers
Storing data on unlocked public computers

q: A company collects customer emails but is not sure how long to keep them. What should it check?
r: Applicable privacy laws and its retention policy
Rules set how long data may be kept.
w: Nothing, because emails can be kept forever
Only the color of the email design

q: What is an internal control?
r: A procedure that protects assets and ensures accurate records
Examples include approvals and reconciliations.
w: A rule that sets the price of a product
A tool for advertising to customers

q: Why should the same person not both approve and pay invoices?
r: It separates duties to reduce the risk of fraud
No one person controls the whole process.
w: It makes payments take longer to complete
It is required for every bank account
It lowers the cost of the invoices

q: What is the Sarbanes-Oxley Act mainly about?
r: Accuracy and honesty in financial reporting by public companies
It followed major accounting scandals.
w: Setting the minimum wage for workers
Rules for food safety in restaurants
Limits on imports from other countries

q: What is a conflict of interest?
r: A situation where personal interests could affect job decisions
Employees should disclose it.
w: A debate about a company's slogan

q: A purchasing manager awards a contract to a company owned by their sibling without telling anyone. What should they have done?
r: Disclose the relationship and step away from the decision
Transparency protects the firm.
w: Keep it secret to avoid questions
Award it anyway because the price was fair
Ask the sibling to hide the ownership

q: What is an ethics hotline?
r: A confidential way for employees to report concerns
It encourages reporting without fear.
w: A number that customers call to place orders
A number used to schedule deliveries
A number used to reset passwords

q: What is a policy?
r: A formal statement of the rules a company expects people to follow
Policies guide decisions.
w: A short-term plan for one project
A list of the goods in storage

q: Why should policies be communicated and enforced consistently?
r: So that all employees understand and are treated fairly
Consistency supports compliance.
w: So that only managers know the rules
So that rules can be ignored when convenient
So that employees do not ask any questions

q: What is a trademark?
r: A word, symbol or design that identifies a brand and is legally protected
Others may not use it without permission.
w: A list of a company's competitors
A mark showing a product was inspected

q: A business uses a competitor's logo on its own products without permission. What law is likely violated?
r: Trademark law
It protects brand identifiers.

q: What is a contract?
r: A legally enforceable agreement between parties
It needs an offer, acceptance and consideration.
w: A friendly promise with no legal weight
A list of a company's products
A message sent to a customer

q: A supplier fails to deliver goods as agreed in a signed contract. What has occurred?
r: A breach of contract
One party failed to perform.
w: The failure is not a success.
A normal delay with no consequences

q: What is an environmental regulation?
r: A rule that limits pollution and protects natural resources
The EPA enforces many of them.
w: A rule that sets the price of energy
A rule that decides employee holidays

q: A factory releases waste into a river without a permit. Which agency is most likely to act?
r: The Environmental Protection Agency
It enforces pollution rules.

q: What is a project?
r: A temporary effort with a defined beginning and end to create a result
It has specific goals and limits.
w: An ongoing task that is repeated every day
A permanent department within a company

q: What is project management?
r: Planning, organizing and controlling resources to complete a project
It aims to meet goals on time and budget.
w: Hiring workers for permanent positions only
Setting the price of a product for sale

q: What is the project scope?
r: The work that is included in the project and what is not
It sets boundaries.
w: The total money spent on the project
The list of everyone on the team
The date the project will end

q: A client asks for extra features partway through a project. What is this called?
r: Scope creep
The scope grows beyond the plan.

q: What is the best way to handle scope creep?
r: Evaluate the change and approve it only through a formal change process
It protects time and budget.
w: Ignore the client and keep working

q: What is a project manager's role?
r: Leading the team and making sure the project meets its goals
They coordinate people and resources.
w: Doing every task in the project alone
Selling the project's results to customers

q: What is a stakeholder in a project?
r: Anyone affected by or interested in the project
Examples include clients, team members and sponsors.
w: Only the person who pays for the project
Only the competitors of the company

q: What is a milestone?
r: A significant point or achievement in a project schedule
It marks progress.
w: A daily task for one team member
The total cost of the project

q: What is a Gantt chart?
r: A bar chart that shows tasks over time
It helps schedule and track work.
w: A pie chart that shows the parts of a budget
A table that lists customers' names
A diagram that shows who reports to whom

q: Which tool best shows when each task starts and ends and how tasks overlap?
r: A Gantt chart
It displays tasks on a timeline.
w: It shows shares of a total.

q: What is the critical path?
r: The longest sequence of dependent tasks that determines the project's minimum length
Delays on it delay the whole project.
w: The shortest route between two offices
The most expensive set of tasks
The list of tasks that can be skipped

q: A task on the critical path is delayed by three days. What happens to the project?
r: The project end date is delayed by three days unless time is made up
Critical tasks drive the schedule.
w: Nothing, because other tasks will catch up automatically
The project finishes three days early

q: What is a project budget?
r: The estimated money needed to complete the project
It is used to control spending.
w: The list of tasks for the project
The group of people working on the project
The date by which the project must end

q: A project is budgeted at $50,000 and has spent $30,000 with 50 percent of the work done. What does this suggest?
r: It may finish over budget
Spending is ahead of progress.
w: It is on track to finish under budget
It has no budget problem at all
Only half the work is done.

q: What is a risk in project management?
r: An uncertain event that could affect the project
It may be positive or negative.
w: A task that is already finished
The final report of the project
The name of the project team

q: A key supplier may deliver late. What should the project manager do?
r: Plan ahead, such as finding a backup supplier
Mitigation reduces the impact.
w: Hope the supplier is on time and do nothing
Remove the task from the plan
Blame the supplier before any delay happens

q: What is a deliverable?
r: A tangible or intangible result that a project must produce
Examples include a report or a product.
w: A task that no one wants to do
A cost that the project must avoid

q: What is the purpose of a kickoff meeting?
r: To start the project by aligning the team on goals and roles
It sets expectations.
w: To end the project and review the results
To collect payment from the customer
To train new customers on the product

q: What is a project charter?
r: A document that formally authorizes a project and states its purpose
It names the sponsor and goals.
w: A list of tasks completed by the team
A final bill sent to a customer
A summary of the project's mistakes

q: Which is the correct order of project phases?
r: Initiate, plan, execute, monitor, close
This follows a typical project life cycle.

q: What happens in the closing phase of a project?
r: The work is finished, results are delivered and lessons are recorded
The project is formally ended.
w: The team is first formed and goals are chosen
Most of the work is done

q: What is a status report?
r: An update on progress, issues and next steps
It keeps stakeholders informed.
w: That is not a status report.

q: Why should project managers communicate regularly with stakeholders?
r: To keep expectations aligned and resolve problems early
Good communication prevents surprises.
w: To keep stakeholders out of decisions

q: What is resource allocation?
r: Assigning people, money and equipment to project tasks
It ensures work can be done.
w: Selling the project's results to customers
Setting prices for the project's products

q: One team member is overloaded while another has no tasks. What should the manager do?
r: Rebalance the workload among team members
Fair allocation improves performance.
w: Remove the overloaded member from the project
That does not solve the issue.
Give the idle member a bonus
That does not solve the issue.

q: What is agile project management?
r: An approach that delivers work in short cycles with frequent feedback
Teams adapt as requirements change.
w: An approach that finishes all planning before any work starts and never changes
An approach that ignores customer input

q: What is a sprint in agile?
r: A short, fixed period in which a team completes a set of work
Sprints often last two weeks.
w: A race between two project teams
A final presentation to the client
A meeting to assign blame for delays

q: A team plans two-week cycles, reviews work with the client and adjusts the plan. Which method is this?
r: Agile
It uses short cycles and feedback.

q: What is the waterfall method?
r: A step-by-step approach where each phase finishes before the next begins
It follows a fixed order.
w: An approach that repeats short cycles with frequent feedback
An approach that has no planning
An approach used only for water projects

q: Which project is best suited to the waterfall method?
r: Building a bridge from fixed plans
Requirements are clear and stable.
w: Developing an app whose features are unclear
Testing a new idea with rapid changes
Exploring a new market with unknown needs

q: What is a work breakdown structure (WBS)?
r: A way of dividing a project into smaller, manageable tasks
It organizes the work.
w: A list of reasons a project failed
A chart of the company's profits
A rule that limits team size

q: Why break a large project into smaller tasks?
r: Smaller tasks are easier to assign, track and estimate
It improves control.
w: It makes the project take longer on purpose
It removes the need for a schedule
It hides the project from stakeholders

q: What is a dependency in a project?
r: A task that cannot start or finish until another task does
Order of work matters.
w: A team member who depends on the manager for pay
A cost that depends on exchange rates
A client who depends on a single product

q: Painting a wall cannot begin until the wall is built. What type of relationship is this?
r: A task dependency
One task relies on another.

q: What is financial information?
r: Data about a business's money, such as income, costs and assets
It helps people make decisions.
w: Data about a business's advertising colors and logos
Data about a business's employee birthdays
Data about a business's office layout

q: What is an income statement?
r: A report of revenue, expenses and profit over a period
It shows performance.
w: A report of assets and liabilities at one date
A report of cash movements by activity
That is a cash flow statement.
A report of changes in owners' equity

q: What is a balance sheet?
r: A report of assets, liabilities and equity at a point in time
It shows financial position.
w: A report of revenue and expenses over a year
A report of cash in and out during a period
That is a cash flow statement.
A report listing a company's customers

q: What is a cash flow statement?
r: A report of cash coming in and going out during a period
It shows operating, investing and financing cash.
w: A report of assets and liabilities on one date
A report of profit after taxes
A report of a company's future sales goals

q: A company has high profit but little cash. Which statement would best show why?
r: The cash flow statement
It tracks real cash movement.

q: What is the accounting equation?
r: Assets equal liabilities plus owner's equity
Every transaction keeps it balanced.

q: A company has assets of $90,000 and liabilities of $35,000. What is owner's equity?
r: Equity is assets minus liabilities.

q: What is double-entry bookkeeping?
r: Recording every transaction in at least two accounts
Debits equal credits.
w: Recording each transaction on two different days
Recording each transaction by two people at once

q: What is a ledger?
r: A record of all the accounts of a business with their balances
Transactions are posted to it.
w: A list of daily sales at a store

q: What is a trial balance?
r: A list of account balances used to check that debits equal credits
It checks the ledger's arithmetic.
w: A test of a new product with customers

q: What is a budget?
r: A plan that estimates income and expenses for a period
It guides spending.
w: A list of owners and partners

q: A department's budget was $20,000 and actual spending was $23,500. What is the variance?
r: $3,500 over budget

q: What is accounts receivable?
r: Money owed to a business by customers for sales on credit
It is a current asset.
w: Money a business owes to suppliers
Cash held in a bank account

q: What is accounts payable?
r: Money a business owes to suppliers for goods bought on credit
It is a current liability.
w: Money the business holds as cash

q: Net credit sales are $240,000 and average receivables are $30,000. What is the receivables turnover?
r: 8 times
$240,000 divided by $30,000 equals 8.

q: What is the current ratio?
r: Current assets divided by current liabilities
It measures short-term liquidity.
w: Total liabilities divided by total assets

q: A company has current assets of $60,000 and current liabilities of $40,000. What is its current ratio?
r: $60,000 divided by $40,000 equals 1.5.

q: What is gross profit?
r: Sales minus the cost of goods sold
It is profit before operating expenses.
w: Sales minus all expenses and taxes
Sales plus the cost of goods sold

q: Sales are $500,000, cost of goods sold is $320,000 and operating expenses are $110,000. What is operating profit?
What is depreciation?
r: Spreading the cost of an asset over its useful life
It reflects wear and age.
w: Increasing the value of an asset over time

q: Equipment costs $12,000, has no salvage value and lasts 5 years. What is straight-line depreciation per year?
r: $12,000 divided by 5 equals $2,400.

q: What is financial forecasting?
r: Estimating future revenues, costs and cash needs
It guides planning.
w: Recording past sales in a ledger

q: Why do lenders request financial statements?
r: To judge whether a business can repay a loan
Statements show profit, debt and cash.

q: What is an audit?
r: An independent examination of financial records
It checks accuracy and compliance.

q: What is GAAP?
r: Generally Accepted Accounting Principles, a set of standard accounting rules
They make statements consistent.
w: A federal program for small businesses

q: Why must businesses follow consistent accounting rules?
r: So that financial statements can be compared and trusted
Consistency supports clarity.
w: So that every business reports the same profit
So that accounting is easier to ignore
So that taxes are never paid

q: What is a financial ratio used for?
r: Comparing figures to judge performance or health
Ratios simplify analysis.

q: Net income is $24,000 on sales of $300,000. What is the profit margin?
r: $24,000 divided by $300,000 equals 0.08.

q: What is data integrity in financial systems?
r: Accuracy and consistency of financial data over its life
It prevents errors and tampering.
w: Storing data in many different formats

q: Which control best protects financial data from unauthorized changes?
r: Role-based access and an audit trail
Only approved users can edit, and changes are logged.
w: Sharing one password among all staff
Allowing anyone to edit any record
